description: "How NCodeGroup .NET code registers, resolves, scopes and composes services with Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection: service lifetimes, TryAdd and TryAddEnumerable, marker-typed registration builders, extension-point shapes, options validation and host start-up ordering."

# Dependency injection

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **In production code, keep singleton services stateless. Keep per-request state on the request (for example `HttpContext.Items` or a request context object), and never memoize it on a singleton.** A value memoized on a singleton (for example `_result ??= await ...`) leaks the first request's answer to every later request. A memoized client-authentication result once let later requests reuse it whatever credentials they presented. *Check:* Look for mutable fields, lazy caches or `??=` assignments on singleton-registered types that are filled from request, user or session data. *Note:* Don't report a singleton that holds a concurrent cache of the application's own data, such as its own client tokens, as long as its keys and values come only from configuration and app-owned credentials and no request or session state goes into it. A singleton that holds the current user or session is acceptable only in a single-user WebAssembly host, and its registration's remarks must say that and name what serves the server or prerendering side. If the same registration also runs on a server host for prerendering, one user's principal can be returned to another. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1381; Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **In production code, never store request or ambient context (`HttpContext`, the request or user, a `ClaimsPrincipal`, a request-scoped `IServiceProvider`) in a field of a long-lived service. Read it where it is used, take it as a parameter, or make the type a live view over `IHttpContextAccessor`.** Captured context goes stale, outlives its request, leaks into other requests and makes the type hard to test. *Check:* Look for fields or properties on singletons or other long-lived services that hold an `HttpContext`, request, user, `ClaimsPrincipal` or scoped `IServiceProvider` captured at construction. *Note:* Don't report a value object created for each call (for example a validation context made by a factory per call or per request) that carries the `HttpContext` to a callee. The rule covers long-lived services, so check the type's lifetime before reporting. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **A singleton that uses scoped services must create a new DI scope for each call or dispatch, through `IServiceScopeFactory`, and resolve those services from that scope. It must never capture scoped services or cache handler instances.** A scoped service captured by a singleton outlives its scope and is shared across every caller. *Check:* Look for singletons that take scoped services in their constructor or keep resolved handler instances, rather than resolving them from a scope created for each call. <sub>Identity ADR-1047</sub>
- **In background work, create an `AsyncServiceScope` (`CreateAsyncScope`) for each unit of work, such as one job attempt or one tenant group. Resolve scoped services and handlers from that scope, not from the root provider. Dispose any request-like context the work creates before the scope is disposed.** Background work has no request scope. Each unit needs its own scoped dependencies and context, and async-disposable services are disposed correctly only by an async scope. *Check:* Look for hosted services or workers that resolve scoped services from the root `IServiceProvider`, reuse one scope across attempts, tenants or the service's whole lifetime, use synchronous `CreateScope`, or don't dispose the context they created. <sub>Identity ADR-1223; Identity ADR-1242; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **An `IValidateOptions<T>` must not depend on the options it validates. It must not take `IOptions<T>`, `IOptionsMonitor<T>` or `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` for the same `T`, and it must not resolve or construct services (for example `IEnumerable<IHandler>`) whose dependency graph reads those options. To list registered names or capabilities, read a descriptor-only catalog that constructs no components.** Reading options from inside their own validation recurses and deadlocks the host while it is composed, in a cycle the container cannot detect. *Check:* Look at the constructor dependencies of each `IValidateOptions<T>` and setting-descriptor source for an options accessor of the same `T`, or for injected services or service collections that depend on it. <sub>Identity ADR-1137; Identity ADR-1145; Identity ADR-1400</sub>
- **In production code, don't put a start-up check that depends on a hosted service's work (such as a warm-up that loads keys) in `ValidateOnStart` or an `IStartupValidator`. Make it a hosted service registered after that hosted service. Put work that must run before every hosted service's `StartAsync` in `IHostedLifecycleService.StartingAsync` instead of relying on registration order.** Every start-up validator runs before any hosted service starts, and every `StartingAsync` runs before any `StartAsync` whatever the registration order. *Check:* Look for `ValidateOnStart`/`IStartupValidator` logic that reads state a hosted service creates, for a gate hosted service that isn't registered after the service it depends on, and for hosted services inserted at index 0 just to run first. <sub>Identity ADR-1247; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a service can only be resolved after a hosted service's start phase has loaded it (for example a keyed key-ring provider), don't resolve it from an eager singleton, an options validator or an existence check. Check existence with a registration query (a `Has…` method) and resolve it only when a request uses it. Document the ordering constraint in the registration's XML summary, and make early resolution throw an `InvalidOperationException` that names what wasn't loaded.** Resolving it early throws at start-up. If the ordering dependency isn't documented, a future early consumer fails in a way that is hard to diagnose. *Check:* Look for `GetRequiredKeyedService` or similar resolution of start-loaded services in singleton constructors, validators or start-up checks, and for DI factories that return state filled in by hosted start methods without a documented constraint and a descriptive failure. <sub>Identity ADR-1479; Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
- **Check whether a named resource exists through the abstraction that resolves it (for example a provider's `Has…` method). Don't query keyed DI (`IServiceProviderIsKeyedService`, `GetKeyedService`) or the underlying store directly.** A host can replace the provider with a source that isn't keyed DI, and a check that bypasses the provider would refuse names the replacement finds. *Check:* Look for validation code that calls keyed-service APIs or the store directly when a provider interface is the seam that resolves the resource. <sub>Identity ADR-1439</sub>
- **In production code, a constructor of a provider or service that validators or capability readers may resolve does no I/O, reads no options and creates no SDK client. Its type's XML documentation says so.** Validators and capability readers can end up resolving such providers, so I/O or option reads in the constructor would run during plain validation. *Check:* Look for `IOptions` access, client construction or network calls in the constructors of key or remote providers and similar services, and check that their XML doc states that the constructor does no I/O. <sub>Identity ADR-1474</sub>
- **A library that decorates a service the host may also register (for example a hasher that ASP.NET Core Identity registers with `TryAdd`) must handle both registration orders. Replace the last non-keyed registration in place, keep its lifetime, and wrap its instance, factory or implementation type. If there is none, add the decorated default. Never wrap a service that is already decorated.** Hosts register the service before or after the library call, and `TryAdd` keeps whichever registration came first. Wrapping twice applies the decoration twice. *Check:* Look for decorator registration that uses only `Add` or `TryAdd`, changes the lifetime, ignores `ImplementationInstance` or `ImplementationFactory`, or has no guard against wrapping twice. <sub>Identity ADR-1238</sub>
- **Don't use `TryAddEnumerable` to register several instances of one implementation type. Give each built-in strategy its own class. For data registered as singleton instances of one record type, register each instance with an instance-aware try-add, or find and replace the existing instance by its identifying key (tag, name).** `TryAddEnumerable` keeps only one registration per implementation type, so it silently drops other instances, such as other curves or algorithm specifications. *Check:* Look for several `TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton(instance))` calls whose instances share a concrete type, or for `TryAddEnumerable` used to dedupe data that should be unique per key. <sub>Identity ADR-1392; Identity ADR-1402; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't ask for `TryAddEnumerable` when several services are registered as instances of one record type and a documented replace-by-key step handles duplicates.** `TryAddEnumerable` can't tell such instances apart. The replace-by-key design is intended, and a duplicate key registered any other way fails loudly at start-up. *Check:* Before reporting, check whether the registrations are instances of one type and whether the registration's doc comment or a decision record describes replacing by key. <sub>Identity outcomes of #548</sub>
- **Create `HttpMessageHandler` instances, including the inner handlers that a stub or wrapper disposes, inside the `ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler` or `AddHttpMessageHandler` factory lambda. Don't create them outside the lambda and capture them.** `IHttpClientFactory` rotates handler chains (every 2 minutes by default) and disposes the old chain. A captured shared handler is already disposed when the next chain uses it, so calls fail with `ObjectDisposedException`. *Check:* Look for handler instances created outside an `IHttpClientFactory` handler factory lambda and captured by it, especially when the wrapping handler disposes them. <sub>Identity outcomes of #465</sub>
- **Send outbound HTTP through a named `IHttpClientFactory` client, not through a private `SocketsHttpHandler`, a raw `new HttpClient` or a custom handler-source interface.** `IHttpClientFactory` is the framework's seam for outbound telemetry, resilience and test-server handlers. A private handler blocks all of them. *Check:* Look for `new SocketsHttpHandler`, `new HttpClient` or bespoke handler sources in outbound code where a named client would do. <sub>Identity ADR-1381</sub>
- **Make a dependency that enforces isolation or security (such as a tenant scope accessor that a DbContext requires) a required constructor parameter, with no optional, nullable or unscoped fallback. Code that constructs the type directly, such as tests and tooling, passes an explicit unscoped implementation.** Isolation has to fail closed. A missing registration must stop the host at start-up, never silently remove isolation. *Check:* Look for isolation dependencies taken as optional or nullable or replaced by an unscoped default, and for direct construction that leaves them out. <sub>Identity ADR-1018</sub>
- **In production code, register a library's default implementation of a service, validator or policy with `TryAdd*` (for example `TryAddSingleton`), not `Add*`, so a host that registers its own implementation replaces it. Register a project's services from one registration class, kept out of the types that do the work.** Integrators must be able to implement, decorate or replace a capability from the composition root without editing the library, and `TryAdd*` lets an earlier registration win. *Check:* Look for `AddSingleton`/`AddScoped`/`AddTransient` of default implementations in a library's registration extensions, for validation or policy logic placed inline in endpoints instead of behind a replaceable service, and for registration code inside working types. Follow the repository's own naming for registration classes. *Note:* Test projects may register stubs and mocks with plain `Add*`. <sub>Identity ADR-1039; Identity ADR-1204; Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1424; Identity ADR-1500; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Register each implementation in an open, multi-implementation collection (event handlers, fan-out command handlers, rules, formatters, blocklists, enrichers, protected-value sources) with `TryAddEnumerable`, and inject the collection as `IEnumerable<T>`.** The collection is open: packages add to it with a single registration, built-ins must not block or replace those additions, and several registration methods may add the same handler, which must still run only once. *Check:* Look for implementations of a multi-registration interface added with `AddSingleton`/`AddScoped`/`AddTransient`, `TryAddSingleton`, or gathered into a hard-coded list instead of with `TryAddEnumerable` (or a repository helper that wraps it). <sub>Identity ADR-1047; Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1112; Identity ADR-1114; Identity ADR-1144; Identity ADR-1201; Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1206; Identity ADR-1236; Identity ADR-1285; Identity ADR-1390; Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **Don't choose behavior with a `switch` or if/else chain over an open vocabulary's names or enum members (authentication methods, code challenge methods, response media types, protected-value holders). Register each member's behavior as its own strategy class and dispatch to the registered strategy by name.** A switch that needs a new case for each extension closes the vocabulary to packages that can't edit it. With strategies, a deployment adds a value by registering one more class. *Check:* Look for switches, if-chains or closed enums that pick an implementation by vocabulary name, for inline branches on response or media type in result or executor code, and for hard-coded lists of stores where a registered strategy collection would do. <sub>Identity ADR-1114; Identity ADR-1144; Identity ADR-1150; Identity ADR-1285; Identity ADR-1289; Identity ADR-1407; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Validate a strategy catalog when it is composed. Its constructor rejects empty names, duplicate names, references to unregistered entries, and implementations without a matching descriptor or descriptors without an implementation, throwing `InvalidOperationException`. Resolve that component in a hosted warm-up at host start, after options validation.** An unnamed strategy isn't advertised, an ambiguous name can be handled by either strategy, and a descriptor without an implementation advertises something that can't work. Checking at composition makes a bad registration fail at start-up, not on the first request. *Check:* Look for name-keyed strategy sets matched lazily at request time, for selection that silently picks one of two duplicate names, and for new strategies added without their descriptor or the reverse. <sub>Identity ADR-1145; Identity ADR-1285; Identity ADR-1289; Identity ADR-1400</sub>
- **When several contributed strategies may handle the same input, pick the one that accepts it and refuse an input that two strategies accept as ambiguous. Use registration order as the host's preference order instead of adding priority numbers to strategies.** Choosing per input keeps the vocabulary open without letting two strategies handle the same key. A priority is a number every contributor would have to choose. *Check:* Look for strategy collections that silently take the first of several matching strategies, or that add a priority or order property to rank contributed strategies. *Note:* This applies to strategy collections. A mediator handler that depends on another handler's effect states its order with handler priorities, not registration order. <sub>Identity ADR-1389; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make registration methods that add to a shared ordered collection produce the same registrations in the same order whatever order the host calls them in. Each method ends by putting the collection into a canonical order that depends only on the set of registered items.** Otherwise a default that falls back to the first item depends on the host's call order. Nothing documents that, and reordering `Program.cs` would change behavior without a test failing. *Check:* Look for `Add*` extensions that append to a shared enumerable registration where the first item becomes the default, and check that tests cover different call orders. <sub>Identity ADR-1402; Identity outcomes of #548</sub>
- **Choose a behavior's DI shape on purpose. A capability that callers invoke to get an answer is a plain service (`IFoo` with a default implementation registered with `TryAddSingleton`) that they call directly. An extension point whose caller iterates over or selects among the implementations is a `TryAddEnumerable` strategy collection. Only a request-pipeline step that consumers must be able to override, or that many independently registered contributors mutate, is an `NCode.Mediator` command sent through the request-scoped `IMediator`.** Each behavior should take the cheapest shape its requirement allows. A mediator dispatch hides its handler, but it adds the priority ordering, post-processing and unified exception handling that real pipeline seams need. *Check:* Look for new command and response-handler pairs whose only caller sends them to get a computed result, for fan-out commands where the caller could loop over `IEnumerable<T>`, and for overridable pipeline steps or shared collections (claims, metadata, validation) built through a directly injected service. *Note:* A conventions file limits the mediator to cross-cutting wrapping. The more specific decision record also allows overridable or multi-contributor pipeline steps, and that is the rule kept here. <sub>Identity ADR-1001; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, when one mediator handler depends on another handler's effect, state the order with `ISupportMediatorPriority`, and do post-processing with `ICommandResponsePostProcessor`. Never rely on registration order or hand-rolled ordering.** Registration order is an invisible, fragile dependency. Handlers run in descending priority order. *Check:* Look for handlers whose correctness assumes they are registered before or after another, or that implement their own ordering or post-processing. <sub>Identity ADR-1001; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make an extension point whose replacement may need I/O asynchronous, and give a deployment-supplied seam a safe default: an inert transport, a resolver that answers 'unknown', or a handler that reports 'unsupported' through a result the caller renders. Register the default with `TryAdd*`. A backend or capability that supports the seam replaces the registration so that the result is the same whatever order the registration methods are called in.** A real policy may need a database or an external lookup. A safe default keeps the protocol correct and secure until a deployment plugs in its own, and a separate optional seam lets a backend that can't support a capability simply say so. *Check:* Look for synchronous pluggable resolver or policy interfaces, defaults that throw `NotImplementedException`, silently succeed, approve or resolve users, or are missing. Also report defaults registered with plain `Add*`, overrides that work only when called before or after the default, and members added to a shared backend interface that most implementations can't honour. *Note:* One earlier decision record has the capability package replace the default with `TryAddSingleton`. That works only when the capability is registered first, so the later rule, an order-independent replacement, is kept. <sub>Identity ADR-1039; Identity ADR-1085; Identity ADR-1086; Identity ADR-1230</sub>
- **Don't let an opt-in capability's registration register a default backend implementation or turn the capability on by default. The host adds the capability and names its backend explicitly.** An opt-in surface that wires no backend makes a host that enables it choose one. *Check:* Look for `TryAdd`/`Add` of a default backend implementation inside the capability's own registration, or for the capability wired by default in base libraries. <sub>Identity ADR-1062</sub>
- **In production code, make a registration extension that hooks, decorates or consumes another library's services extend the marker-typed service builder returned by that library's registration, specifically the library whose services it actually resolves. Don't make it extend a bare `IServiceCollection` or a lower library's builder.** The receiver type proves at compile time that the prerequisite library, and everything beneath it, is registered. A bare collection turns a missing prerequisite into a confusing runtime failure. *Check:* Look at the `this` parameter of new `Add*` extensions for dependent capabilities: is it `IServiceCollection`, or the builder of a library other than the one whose services the package calls? <sub>Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1062; Identity ADR-1069; Identity ADR-1390; Identity ADR-1405; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, take a bare `IServiceCollection` receiver only for registrations that stand alone: chain roots that start a builder with no prerequisite, one-service or generic utility helpers, and marker-less cross-cutting infrastructure. Make a helper that several libraries' builders call extend the repository's non-generic service builder, not a bare collection or one library's marker builder.** A registration should do the right thing even if it were the only one registered. The non-generic builder still requires the caller to hold some library's builder without tying the helper to one library. *Check:* For each new bare-collection extension, ask whether it depends on another library's services. For shared helpers (message factories, endpoint providers), check that they extend the non-generic builder. <sub>Identity ADR-1069; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Express a registration's second prerequisite as a required parameter of that prerequisite's marker-typed builder, the one its registration returned. Don't use a marker struct value, an optional or nullable builder, or a custom proof type, and return the receiver builder.** Anyone can `default` an empty marker struct, so a marker value proves nothing. Only a builder minted by the prerequisite's registration can't be forged, and returning the receiver keeps the chain on the primary library. *Check:* Look at registration methods with an extra prerequisite for a marker-typed, optional or nullable, or custom proof parameter, and for a return type other than the receiver. <sub>Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1057; Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **Make every registration that another registration depends on, including a dependency-inverted seam such as a custom store, mint and return its own marker-typed builder.** Dependents can demand an unforgeable proof of registration only if the prerequisite's registration hands one back. *Check:* Look for store and seam registrations that dependents need but that return `void`, the bare collection or a plain builder. <sub>Identity ADR-1051; Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **Define a registration marker as an empty `readonly struct` that implements the repository's registration-marker interface, and put it in the library's `.Abstractions` package.** The marker's type identity is the whole signal, so it carries no data to keep in sync, and abstractions-only consumers must be able to name the builder without referencing the implementation. *Check:* Look for new marker types that are classes, carry members or data, or are declared in an implementation package. <sub>Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **Encode registration prerequisites only in the builder types. Don't add runtime checks that another library was registered, and don't make an opt-in library check whether it is registered itself (for example by returning 501 when a feature is missing).** Runtime checks delay an avoidable mistake to start-up or request time and depend on order. Typed builders make a missing prerequisite a compile error, and once a library is opt-in, being registered is what makes it present. *Check:* Look for registration code that inspects the service collection (`Any(d => d.ServiceType == …)`, `IsRegistered`) or throws to signal a missing library, and for endpoints that probe the container for their own registration or return 501 Not Implemented. <sub>Identity ADR-1057; Identity ADR-1069</sub>
- **Don't ask a registration method to register, require or validate a dependency when some of its callers (such as migration workers or design-time DbContext factories) only build a model and never resolve the service that needs it.** Requiring the dependency would force an unused service onto those hosts. A host that does resolve the service without it still gets a DI error that names the missing type. *Check:* Before reporting a dependency that fails only when resolved, find every caller of the registration method and check whether some never resolve the dependent service, and whether the XML doc says the host supplies it. <sub>Identity outcomes of #807</sub>
- **In production code, have the package that owns a feature register the framework and infrastructure services its own services need (routing, `IHttpClientFactory`, authentication, `AddDataProtection()`, `AddMetrics()`, `TimeProvider.System`) with `TryAdd*` or the framework's idempotent `Add*` call.** Composing a feature should be turnkey. Host wiring that works only because an unrelated service (such as `AddControllers`) pulled a dependency in breaks when that service is removed, and `TryAdd` keeps a host's own `TimeProvider`, such as a test clock. *Check:* Look for packages that consume such services without registering them, for hosts that depend on unrelated `Add*` calls for side effects, and for `AddSingleton<TimeProvider>` that overrides the host's provider. *Note:* Don't suggest moving such a registration (for example `AddMetrics()`) out to the host. This is different from host-wide stores such as `IDistributedCache`, which a library never registers. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1247; Identity outcomes of #529</sub>
- **In library code, don't register host-wide infrastructure such as `IDistributedCache` or another shared cache or store, and don't call last-wins host configuration such as Kestrel's `ConfigureHttpsDefaults`. Depend on the library's own ports and let the composition root choose the adapter and TLS settings.** A library registration decides shared infrastructure for the host and every other consumer, and `ConfigureHttpsDefaults` keeps only its last action, so a package would silently replace the host's HTTPS defaults or be replaced by them. *Check:* Look for `AddDistributedMemoryCache`, `AddStackExchangeRedisCache`, `ConfigureKestrel` or `ConfigureHttpsDefaults` inside a library's service-collection extensions. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity ADR-1202; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a library registers an authentication scheme, never override the host's default. Register it as a named scheme and make it the default only when the host hasn't set one.** Overriding the host's default scheme would silently change how its other endpoints authenticate. *Check:* Look for `AddAuthentication(scheme)` or unconditional assignments to `DefaultScheme`, `DefaultChallengeScheme` or `DefaultAuthenticateScheme` in library or capability registration code. *Note:* An earlier decision record says a capability's authentication cookie scheme is always registered as a named scheme and never made the default. Follow that for such capability cookie schemes. <sub>Identity ADR-1062; Identity ADR-1292</sub>
- **Reach a behavioral hook that the host configures at start-up (a delegate) through the abstraction-level type that declares it, not by injecting `IOptions<T>` of an implementation package's options.** Injecting the implementation's options ties the consumer to that package and is impossible from abstractions-only packages, so each surface ends up implementing the hook its own way and the host's override is honored in some places only. *Check:* Look for new `IOptions<…Options>` injections used only to read a behavioral delegate, for abstractions-only consumers that reimplement a hook, and check that a new hook is declared on the abstraction and wired from the options in the implementation. <sub>Identity ADR-1053</sub>
- **In production code, an implementation package references only `.Abstractions` packages and foundation packages, never another implementation package. Cross-implementation collaboration goes through an abstraction resolved from DI, and the concrete type is referenced only in a composition root or host.** Implementation-to-implementation references bring transitive dependencies, make the package boundary meaningless and lose independent replaceability. *Check:* Look at `ProjectReference`/`PackageReference` changes in implementation `.csproj` files for non-`.Abstractions`, non-foundation implementation projects that aren't composition roots or hosts. *Note:* A documented layered framework reference is allowed, such as an Entity Framework slice that references the EF framework it plugs into. <sub>Identity ADR-1500; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Keep library packages dependent only on `System.Diagnostics` and `System.Diagnostics.Metrics` for telemetry, and set up the OpenTelemetry SDK and exporters in the host-composition package, not in libraries or `Program.cs`.** Recording costs nothing until a listener subscribes, and putting the host together is the composition package's job. *Check:* Look for OpenTelemetry SDK package references in library projects, or OpenTelemetry pipeline setup written directly in `Program.cs`. <sub>Identity ADR-1197</sub>
- **Keep `Program.cs` a flat list of `AddX`, `UseX` and `MapX` calls. Move any `if`, loop, policy builder, `new`, constant or configuration read into an extension in the owning project, leaving only host-specific inputs such as the database provider and connection string, production secrets and Kestrel HTTPS defaults.** Composition stays readable and features stay turnkey. *Check:* Look for logic, literals or configuration reads added to `Program.cs`. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, constructor-inject every dependency. Don't `new` a collaborator inside a method or create a private instance of a type registered as a shared singleton (such as a lock table). Use service location (`RequestServices`, `GetService`, `GetRequiredService`, `GetServices`) only when a singleton resolves a scoped or open-generic collaborator, or a service chosen by a generic type argument, at the point of use, or in framework glue marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`.** Injected dependencies keep code testable and lifetimes explicit. Private instances can't be substituted, and injecting the shared one later would silently merge key spaces that were kept apart only by convention. *Check:* Look for `new` of service collaborators, fields initialised with `new()` for types also registered as singletons, and service-locator calls outside the allowed cases. When separate users share an injected instance, check that their keys include a purpose component. *Note:* In test projects, constructing the code under test and a private sealed nested stub that one test file needs is expected. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #520</sub>
- **In production code, register a stateless capability as a singleton and run a long-running loop as `AddHostedService<T>` over a `BackgroundService`, with DI wiring kept out of the type that does the work.** Consistent lifetimes, and work types that stay constructor-injectable and testable. *Check:* Look for stateless services registered as scoped or transient, loops started outside a hosted service, and worker types that register themselves or resolve services from a provider. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, prefer an instance service behind an interface, registered as a singleton, to a `static` utility class. Keep `static` for pure functions, constants, extension entry points and immutable thread-safe shared instances such as a cached `JsonSerializerOptions`, and never use static mutable or ambient state.** Static utilities that have dependencies can't be substituted in tests, and static mutable state leaks between callers. *Check:* Look for new static classes that hold dependencies or do I/O, and for mutable static fields. *Note:* Don't report a static helper that is a pure function of its arguments, builds on sibling static helpers, and gets its side-effecting dependencies (such as a logger) from the caller, for example through a delegate. Callers' tests still cover it through their own mocks. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #835</sub>
- **Enumerate an injected `IEnumerable<T>` only once: copy it into an array or `ImmutableArray` and build any index from that copy.** A lazy or non-repeatable sequence can yield different items each time, leaving the list and the index disagreeing. *Check:* Look for constructors that enumerate an injected `IEnumerable<T>` more than once, for example a collection expression plus a separate index build. <sub>Identity outcomes of #548</sub>
- **Document in a registration method's remarks when it removes services the host registered (for example `RemoveAll<T>()` then `Add`), saying that it replaces them and why.** A host that registered its own implementation earlier would otherwise lose it without notice. *Check:* Look for `RemoveAll` or `Replace` calls in `Add*` extensions with no matching remarks. <sub>Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **Don't report an object disposed both by the DI container and by another owner when both dispose paths are idempotent and the second owner is needed to dispose instances that never go through the container.** Idempotent disposal can't throw or release resources twice, and the extra owner covers instances the container never created. *Check:* Before reporting, read the `Dispose`/`DisposeAsync` implementations (for example an `IsDisposed` guard) and check whether some instances bypass the container factory. <sub>Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
- **Don't report a `TryAdd*` registration as unused or duplicate when a service that the same registration method registers depends on it through its constructor. When sibling registration methods repeat the same block of shared `TryAdd*` registrations, suggest moving it into one private helper that both call.** The registration lets the method work when nothing else registers the dependency, and identical `TryAdd*` registrations can't conflict. A repeated list, though, can drift apart. *Check:* Trace the constructor dependencies of the services the method adds and check that the duplicates are all `TryAdd*` of the same implementation. Look for repeated `TryAddSingleton`/`TryAddScoped`/`TryAddTransient` blocks in sibling methods. <sub>Identity outcomes of #599; Identity outcomes of #629</sub>
- **Remove constructor-injected dependencies that the class stores but never reads.** A dead dependency makes readers check it for nothing and makes DI resolve a service for nothing. *Check:* Look for constructor parameters or properties (such as a `TimeProvider` carried over from copied code) that no member of the class reads. *Note:* A parameter the repository's conventions require, such as a `CancellationToken` on every async method, isn't dead code. <sub>Identity outcomes of #555</sub>
- **In a test project, name every `IServiceCollection` local, parameter and lambda parameter `serviceCollection`. An `IServiceProvider` keeps its own name.** This matches the production naming rule, so a service collection has the same name everywhere. *Check:* Look in test code for `IServiceCollection` variables or lambda parameters named `services`, `s`, `collection` or anything other than `serviceCollection`. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-testing.instructions.md</sub>
